name: Toys Safety Directive
evidence_rating: thin: Commission impact assessments and evaluation only; no data on injuries and no independent studies found
summary: The 2009 directive tightened safety and chemical rules for toys sold in the EU. The Commission's 2020 evaluation found intra-EU toy trade grew about 60% and compliance costs were modest (about 2% of turnover once), but one in three inspected toys broke the rules and there are no data on whether child injuries fell. A replacement regulation is forecast to avoid EUR 240 million to 1.2 billion a year in health damage.

indicators.objective: The 2008 proposal has no indicators section; the 2020 evaluation notes the Directive set no monitoring indicators, so data are incomplete and not comparable

indicators.indicator: Stricter chemical and other safety requirements; fewer accidents
indicators.evidence: No data on accidents or injuries; one in three toy samples inspected by market surveillance is non-compliant; chemical limits judged deficient (age limit 36 months, CMR derogations).
Intra-EU toy exports rose about 60% after full application in 2013; number of toy companies +10% in 5 years (not attributed causally).
One-off costs about 2% of annual turnover, recovered within about 3 years; recurring costs ~7% higher than predecessor; adaptations ~1% of turnover.

indicators.indicator: Generic bans on most harmful chemicals; digital product passport
indicators.target_or_baseline: Health benefits EUR 240m-1.2bn/yr (endocrine disruptors alone); one-off costs EUR 23.5-397m

literature.citation: European Commission (2008), Executive summary of the impact assessment for the proposal on the safety of toys, SEC(2008) 39
literature.title: Executive summary of the impact assessment for the proposal on the safety of toys
literature.method: ex-ante (three external studies, consultation of 1,500+ respondents)
literature.headline: Revised directive preferred to repeal or 'old approach'; ban on CMR substances in accessible parts expected to raise manufacturing costs but bring considerable long-term health benefits (assessed in DALYs); warnings costs expected lower than industry claims; benefits not measurable in detail
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected tighter toy rules to raise costs somewhat but deliver large, hard-to-measure health gains for children.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Evaluation of Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys (executive summary SWD(2020) 288), SWD(2020) 287
literature.title: Evaluation of Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys (executive summary SWD(2020) 288)
literature.method: evaluation (2015 external study, JRC cost-benefit study, consultations, national reports)
literature.headline: More effective than the 1988 directive, but deficient on chemicals; one in three inspected samples non-compliant; intra-EU exports +60% since 2012/13; one-off costs ~2% of turnover recovered in 3 years or less; toy firms +10% in 5 years; benefits not quantifiable for lack of accident data; no monitoring indicators
literature.summary_plain: The 2020 evaluation found toy trade flourished and costs were modest, but a third of inspected toys broke the rules and there is no data on whether injuries fell.

literature.citation: European Commission (2023), Impact assessment for the proposal for a Toy Safety Regulation (executive summary SWD(2023) 270), SWD(2023) 269
literature.title: Impact assessment for the proposal for a Toy Safety Regulation (executive summary SWD(2023) 270)
literature.headline: Generic bans on harmful chemicals: health benefits EUR 240m-1.2bn a year for endocrine disruptors alone; one-off redesign costs EUR 23.5-396.66m; testing +EUR 7.3-11.7m a year; EUR 249-367m of products could be affected; digital passport saves industry EUR 13-20m a year in inspections
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the new toy rules to avoid EUR 240 million to 1.2 billion a year of health damage from hormone-disrupting chemicals alone.
